column4: The section names the root ه د ي (“to guide”) and insists the ridges are visible before the choice; here “هَدَيْنَاهُ السَّبِيلَ” is followed by grateful or ungrateful travelers, so failure lies in response to a shown way.
The section treats the two ridges as opposed ways of response; “فُجُورَهَا وَتَقْوَاهَا” gives the soul the corresponding paired moral alternatives.
The section’s two visible routes issue in divergent action; “إِنَّ سَعْيَكُمْ لَشَتَّىٰ” explicitly says human striving takes different courses.
The section links the pass to costly, outward good; this branch begins “مَنْ أَعْطَىٰ وَاتَّقَىٰ,” giving and guarding oneself as one route.
The section makes the hill a chosen response after guidance; this ayah adds the giver’s belief in “الْحُسْنَىٰ,” which underlies that trustful action.
The section’s path demands effort, while this branch promises “لِلْيُسْرَىٰ” for the giver who believes and gives; it shows divine facilitation at the end of that course.
The section rules out lack of a guide as the reason for not starting; “إِنَّ عَلَيْنَا لَلْهُدَىٰ” states God’s responsibility for guidance within the same two-course passage.
The section explicitly names root ع ق ب for an end or recompense and sets it beside patience and spending; this ayah joins both acts to “عُقْبَى الدَّارِ,” the final outcome of the abode.
The section links patient passage through hardship to its end; the greeting “بِمَا صَبَرْتُمْ” culminates in “فَنِعْمَ عُقْبَى الدَّارِ,” the same root-family outcome.
The section’s pass is a hard ascent one must choose to enter; after 74:11–16 introduces a richly endowed denier, this ayah makes his ascent forced: “سَأُرْهِقُهُ صَعُودًا.”
The section says the person did not “iqtahama” the pass; “مُّقْتَحِمٌ مَّعَكُمْ” uses the same root for a crowd plunging into the Fire, reversing the refused ascent into an assault on ruin.
The section’s dictionary gloss of ق ح م includes falling from high to low; after the weighing in this surah, “فَأُمُّهُ هَاوِيَةٌ” makes the failed end a downward plunge.
The section turns the pass toward feeding hungry people; here those who conceal revelation “يَأْكُلُونَ فِي بُطُونِهِمْ إِلَّا النَّارَ,” a reversal in which eating ends in Fire.
The section cites the secondary sense of ص ب ر as daring, not steadfast restraint; “فَمَا أَصْبَرَهُمْ عَلَى النَّارِ” turns that capacity toward the Fire after the preceding ayah’s warning.
This ayah gathers the section’s concrete moral route into one account: freeing people, giving to kin, orphan, and needy, then “الصَّابِرِينَ فِي الْبَأْسَاءِ وَالضَّرَّاءِ.”
The section says hardship is already human ground and the climb must be entered willingly; this asks whether people think they will enter the Garden before affliction and shaking have come.
The section insists that not taking the pass does not remove hardship; “مَعَ الْعُسْرِ يُسْرًا” places ease alongside it.

This adjacent ayah repeats the ease-with-hardship promise, completing the passage’s insistence that hardship does not stand alone; its contribution is the reiterated assurance “إِنَّ مَعَ الْعُسْرِ يُسْرًا.”
This is a nonlexical parallel: the section says its named root ك ب د differs from this root, but both stage purposeful toil; “كَادِحٌ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ كَدْحًا” directs exertion toward meeting God.
The section defines patience as holding the self back from panic; “خُلِقَ هَلُوعًا” names the contrasting human disposition the climb must resist.
The section contrasts steadiness on the pass with panic; this ayah specifies that the person is “إِذَا مَسَّهُ الشَّرُّ جَزُوعًا,” crying out when harm touches him.

The section’s day of hunger and fatigue, spent wealth, and counsel of patience meet in this test of “الْجُوعِ ... وَنَقْصٍ مِّنَ الْأَمْوَالِ”; hardship names concrete conditions, not an abstract obstacle.

The section labels as a secondary dictionary sense of ع ق ب turning back on one’s heels; this ayah says “نَرُدُّ عَلَىٰ أَعْقَابِنَا بَعْدَ إِذْ هَدَانَا اللَّهُ,” making retreat after guidance the precise opposite of entering the pass.

The section describes an uphill exertion and a body that must enter difficulty; here a tight chest is likened to “يَصَّعَّدُ فِي السَّمَاءِ,” within an ayah explicitly contrasting divine guidance and misguidance.
The section says guidance has already been shown and the missing act is striving; God says of those who strive, “لَنَهْدِيَنَّهُمْ سُبُلَنَا,” joining exertion to being guided on paths.
The section says the person cannot excuse refusal as an unseen route; of Thamud, “فَهَدَيْنَاهُمْ فَاسْتَحَبُّوا الْعَمَىٰ عَلَى الْهُدَىٰ” makes rejection after guidance explicit.
The section’s two ridges become a choice after the way is shown; this ayah commands “هَٰذَا صِرَاطِي مُسْتَقِيمًا” and warns that other paths scatter people from it.
The section makes a mountain pass the physical scene of a demanded crossing; here pilgrims answer the call by coming “مِن كُلِّ فَجٍّ عَمِيقٍ,” traversing far, deep passes toward the House.
This ayah supplies the setting for 76:3’s shown road: humanity is created from a mixed drop “نَّبْتَلِيهِ,” so the choice of route occurs within a trial.
After 13:22 names “عُقْبَى الدَّارِ,” this adjacent ayah makes that outcome concrete as gardens entered with righteous family; it contributes the destination beyond the pass.
After 101:9 calls the fallen person’s end “هَاوِيَةٌ,” this question asks what that abyss is; its role is to open the answer supplied by 101:11.
This is the answer to 101:10’s question about the downward end in 101:9: “نَارٌ حَامِيَةٌ” identifies the abyss as a blazing Fire.
Following the hunger and wealth-loss trial in 2:155, this ayah gives the response “إِنَّا لِلَّهِ وَإِنَّا إِلَيْهِ رَاجِعُونَ,” a way of holding steady through affliction.
This completes the trial-and-response sequence after 2:155–156: God’s blessing, mercy, and the description “هُمُ الْمُهْتَدُونَ” connect patient endurance to guidance.

The section asks for a deliberate climb rather than imagining the destination without passage; this asks whether people expect to enter the Garden before God makes evident those who strive and remain patient.
The section says the route is placed before the person; “قَدْ جَاءَكُم بَصَائِرُ مِن رَّبِّكُمْ” and the ensuing seeing/blindness distinction make sight and responsibility after evidence explicit.
The section’s image is of alternatives already shown; this ayah says “قَصْدُ السَّبِيلِ” belongs to God while some ways turn aside, giving a direct straight/deviant-path boundary.
Against boasting of wealth without taking the difficult way, this describes one who desires the Hereafter and “سَعَىٰ لَهَا سَعْيَهَا”; the effort of that believer is accepted.
The section presents wealth put to effort for hungry and needy people; “وَآتِ ذَا الْقُرْبَىٰ حَقَّهُ” directs resources toward relatives and the vulnerable rather than boastful disposal.
The section names root ه ل ك in the boast “I consumed heaps of wealth”; this ayah’s “وَلَا تُبَذِّرْ تَبْذِيرًا” directly marks wasteful spending as the contrary course.
The section hears the boast of spent wealth as wealth falling into a gap; this garden owner watches his produce destroyed and turns his hands over what he had spent, making loss and regret visible.
The section explicitly names ع ق ب for the end and recompense; after the garden’s ruin, this ayah says God is “خَيْرٌ عُقْبًا,” locating the true final outcome beyond worldly property.
The section’s pass is expressed in aid to the vulnerable; this ayah condemns failing to honor the orphan, a direct reversal of the care that marks the good route.
The section’s route includes feeding on a hungry day; “وَلَا تَحَاضُّونَ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ” condemns the opposite social act.
Against the section’s giving toward need, this ayah depicts consuming inheritance “أَكْلًا لَّمًّا,” an image of taking wealth in rather than using it for others.
The section separates meaningful giving from a boast about heaps of property; “تُحِبُّونَ الْمَالَ حُبًّا جَمًّا” names attachment to wealth as a contrary orientation.
This ayah’s “يَدُعُّ الْيَتِيمَ” (repelling the orphan) reverses the section’s route of mercy toward the orphan.
The section feeds the hungry and needy; “وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ” gives the direct contrary, failure even to urge that food be given.
The section distinguishes wealth poured away from effort that relieves hunger; this gives the contrasting image of spending for God’s cause as a seed multiplied many times over.

A branch of the section’s root ب ل د describes a horse left behind the front-runners; this ayah pictures believers “يُسَارِعُونَ فِي الْخَيْرَاتِ” and “سَابِقُونَ,” the active opposite of lagging at the pass.
The section’s hand-turned millstone makes hardship a continuing exertion; after the ease promised in 94:5–6, this ayah says “فَإِذَا فَرَغْتَ فَانصَبْ,” directing the person to keep striving.
This completes the exertion in 94:7 by directing it toward God: “وَإِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ فَارْغَب,” giving the climb its orientation.

The section’s dictionary account of ق ح م includes throwing oneself into a severe situation; in the context of spending and doing good, this ayah warns “وَلَا تُلْقُوا بِأَيْدِيكُمْ إِلَى التَّهْلُكَةِ,” setting a boundary between the moral climb and reckless self-destruction.

After the ruined garden in 18:42, this ayah compares worldly life to water after which vegetation dries and becomes wind-scattered stubble; it extends the section’s image of wealth and effort falling away.

The section names ع ق ب as the end and distinguishes a difficult moral route from wasted wealth; this ayah contrasts worldly wealth and children with “الْبَاقِيَاتُ الصَّالِحَاتُ” that are better in reward and hope.

The section’s dictionary family ن ج د begins with height, while ع ق ب names the final outcome; this ayah joins refusal of “عُلُوًّا فِي الْأَرْضِ” to the statement that the good outcome belongs to the mindful.

A branch of the section’s root ب ل د describes a horse lagging behind the frontrunners; this oath opens with horses charging and panting, giving the forward-moving scene against which that laggard is defined.

The section’s dictionary branches define ك ب د as entering the middle and ق ح م as plunging into the center of a fearful severity; this ayah’s charging horses reach “فَوَسَطْنَ بِهِ جَمْعًا,” a concrete image of penetration into the middle.
The section says مسغبة is hunger joined to fatigue; on a journey, Moses asks for food and says “لَقَدْ لَقِينَا مِن سَفَرِنَا هَٰذَا نَصَبًا,” joining a meal to travel-weariness.
The section gives ع ق ب the secondary sense of turning back on one’s heels; after the journey-fatigue in 18:62, Moses and his companion retrace their route: “فَارْتَدَّا عَلَىٰ آثَارِهِمَا قَصَصًا.”
The section makes strenuous, chosen passage central to the moral road; “وَأَن لَّيْسَ لِلْإِنسَانِ إِلَّا مَا سَعَىٰ” states that a person’s own striving is what counts.

Following the claim in 53:39, this ayah says “وَأَنَّ سَعْيَهُ سَوْفَ يُرَىٰ”; it adds that the person’s striving will be seen, fitting the section’s insistence that the path is exposed and action is accountable.

This completes the striving passage after 53:39–40: “ثُمَّ يُجْزَاهُ الْجَزَاءَ الْأَوْفَىٰ” gives the full recompense that corresponds to the section’s root-family link between the pass and its final outcome.
The section defines patience as holding the self back from panic; “وَنَهَى النَّفْسَ عَنِ الْهَوَىٰ” describes deliberate restraint of the self, joined here to fear of standing before the Lord.
This completes 79:40’s self-restraint with its stated destination: “فَإِنَّ الْجَنَّةَ هِيَ الْمَأْوَىٰ,” an end reached by resisting desire.
After 91:8 names the soul’s opposing tendencies, this ayah says “قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن زَكَّاهَا,” identifying success with purifying the self rather than stopping at the fork.
This completes the paired outcomes after 91:8–9: “وَقَدْ خَابَ مَن دَسَّاهَا” makes the failed course the contrary to self-purification.
The section’s path leads to feeding the hungry, orphan, and poor; this ayah directly stages feeding “مِسْكِينًا وَيَتِيمًا وَأَسِيرًا,” adding the captive to that concrete charitable route.
After the feeding act in 76:8, this ayah says they feed only for God’s sake and seek neither repayment nor thanks; it distinguishes costly aid from the boast of having spent much.
This continues the motive in 76:9: those who feed fear a grim day, linking the section’s hard, present act to its final reckoning.
After the fear in 76:10, this ayah says God protects them from that day’s evil; it supplies the divine response to the section’s patient passage through hardship.
This completes the feeding-and-recompense sequence: “وَجَزَاهُم بِمَا صَبَرُوا جَنَّةً” explicitly joins patience to the Garden, the outcome beyond the section’s climb.

The section’s root ن ج د carries elevation and height; this ayah warns against walking proudly and says a person will not reach the mountains in height, setting a limit on arrogant claims of mastery over the terrain.

The section presents feeding on a day of hunger; this ayah says God “أَطْعَمَهُم مِّن جُوعٍ” and secured Quraysh from fear, turning the scene around to show the divine provision that human feeding answers.
Alongside the section’s food on a day of hunger, this fasting ayah names “فِدْيَةٌ طَعَامُ مِسْكِينٍ,” a concrete obligation to feed a needy person in the setting of abstention and capacity.

The section stresses real hardship while describing a demanded moral ascent; this closing prayer supplies a capacity boundary: “لَا يُكَلِّفُ اللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا,” so the difficult path is not an impossible burden.
